subtype: Approach: uses a decision matrix when several options are close and reasons must be shown [Thinking]
passage:
I'm Disha, and you asked how we chose the packaging vendor. There were three close ones, and any of them could have worked. I knew that if I simply said, this one, somebody would take it as my favourite.
So before looking at the offers, the team agreed on five things that mattered: price, delivery time, quality of samples, support and payment terms. We each scored every vendor separately out of ten, and I averaged the scores. Vendor B won by two points, mostly on delivery time.
Bhupen, who had wanted vendor C, still disagreed. But he could look at the sheet and see why, and he said, "Fine, the numbers are fair." Nobody called it personal preference, because it wasn't.

qa.q: How many things did the team agree on before looking at the offers?
qa.a: The team agreed on five things that mattered.

qa.q: What did Disha worry about when choosing between the close vendors?
qa.a: Disha worried that someone would take a plain pick as a personal favourite, so wanted reasons that could be seen.

qa.q: What else could Disha do if two vendors ended with the same score?
qa.a: Disha could ask the team which criterion matters most and weigh it more, since a tie needs a shared reason and not a private hunch.

qa.q: How did Bhupen react to the result?
qa.a: Bhupen had wanted vendor C and still disagreed, but could see the scores and accepted that the numbers were fair.

grounding: A manager choosing between three vendors scores them on agreed criteria so the decision can be explained and is not seen as personal preference.

subtype: Approach: uses a decision matrix when several options are close and reasons must be shown [Thinking]
passage: I sit two desks from Rashmi, so I saw most of it. Our office needed a new catering firm, and three had come close: one cheaper, one nearer, one with better marks from the staff tasting. People had favourites. Arun from accounts kept saying the nearer one was obviously best. On Tuesday Rashmi called four of us into the small room. "Kalyani, can you put the sheet on the screen?" she asked me. The columns had been agreed the week before: food quality, price, reliability, hygiene record. Each of us scored, and she added the numbers in front of everyone. The firm from the staff tasting came out on top by two points. Arun looked unhappy, so Rashmi walked him through each column, one by one. I can't say whether she had a favourite of her own. If she did, it never showed; the sheet did the talking.

qa.q: Which criteria were in the columns of the sheet?
qa.a: Food quality, price, reliability and hygiene record.

qa.q: What might Rashmi have been worried about when she added the numbers in front of everyone?
qa.a: She was probably wary of the choice looking like personal favouritism, especially with Arun pushing the nearer firm, so she wanted everyone to see how it was reached.

qa.q: What else could Rashmi do if two firms had tied on the sheet?
qa.a: She could run a short trial week with both, so real experience breaks the tie instead of a gut feeling.

qa.q: How does Arun likely see the result?
qa.a: Arun is disappointed that the nearer firm lost, but because the scores were added in the open, he can see it was not simply Rashmi's preference.

grounding: Shows, through a coworker's eyes, a manager scoring three close catering firms on agreed criteria so the choice can be explained and not seen as personal.

subtype: Approach: uses a decision matrix when several options are close and reasons must be shown [Thinking]
passage:
Monday. Three transport firms had quoted almost the same, and Imran overheard Rajni murmur near the printer that he'd pick the one run by his old college friend. He went home thinking: if I just choose, nobody will believe it wasn't friendship.
Wednesday. He booked the meeting room with Rajni and the two dispatch supervisors. Before anyone looked at the firms' names, they agreed on four things that mattered: on-time record, damaged parcels, price, and how fast each firm answers a call. They scored each firm from one to five on each. His friend's firm came second.
The following Monday, Imran showed the sheet to the regional director. When asked why the friend's firm had lost, he pointed at the damaged-parcels row. Rajni, sitting beside him, added, "We set the criteria together. I'd have picked the same."

qa.q: How did they score each firm?
qa.a: They scored each firm from one to five on each of the four things.

qa.q: What was Imran feeling on Monday, and why?
qa.a: Imran was uneasy that people would think the choice was about friendship, since Rajni had hinted he'd pick his old college friend's firm.

qa.q: What small step would help if the team had disagreed about the criteria?
qa.a: Settle the criteria and how much each one counts before scoring any firm, so the argument is about what matters rather than about which firm people like.

qa.q: How does Rajni see the decision by the following Monday?
qa.a: Rajni has moved from suspicion to trust; having helped set the criteria, Rajni feels able to back the choice openly in front of the director.

grounding: Shows a manager scoring three close transport firms on agreed criteria over several days so the decision can be explained and not seen as favouritism.
